entries.intent: Define reusable parts from a relative anchor; instantiate them with explicit translation, discrete rotation or mirroring, and preserve occupied target structure with a non-air placement mask.
Establish large terrain form first, smooth and connect it second, and add bounded deterministic texture last; checkpoint before every bulk pass.
Use close evaluation for entrances and joins and distant compressed evaluation for silhouette, proportion, palette blocks and context; do not rely on showcase lighting alone.
Organize related materials as an ordered hue, value or temperature ramp with a deliberate direction instead of sampling an unordered random pool.
Validate the exterior shell before the interior pass; keep hidden lighting and other utility blocks on a separate layer that cannot leak into visible surfaces.
Reuse semantic components with their allowed orientation, connection and state fields, not only a block ID, and bind each component to its architectural role.
Assign frame, support, infill, surface and accent materials by per-face texture direction, continuity, border strength and visual weight rather than rarity or game name.
At small scale prioritize individual texture joins and available stair, slab and wall shapes; at large scale and distance prioritize the composition of major color fields.
Extract a source module only after its mass, opening and structural role work in the whole; record connection faces and repair gaps, overlaps, corners and support lines after transformation.
Keep repeated instances visibly related while varying selected width, height, opening, material or detail-density parameters; decoration must not conceal a weak repeated shell.
Give roof, frame, infill, base and accent explicit palette roles; use coordinated value contrast so structural lines remain readable without unrelated high-contrast noise.
Separate the building from ground and neighboring masses through value, hue, saturation or edge contrast; repeat a focal accent more quietly in subordinate locations so it reads as intentional.
Vary the proportions of role-bearing secondary masses, overlap them or share connection faces with the primary mass, and verify that the hierarchy remains readable from primary and corner views.
Partition oversized continuous walls with subordinate entrance, room, tower, dormer or shed volumes, concentrate detail at joins and focal areas, and preserve deliberate blank surfaces elsewhere.
Make tall masses, overhangs and links read as supported through a wider or stepped base, adjacent lower masses, or an explicit support path; do not invent a universal numeric ratio.

Assign every void a visible composition or spatial purpose and choose its base, middle, corner, top or full-layer position accordingly; reject cuts that flatten useful articulation or reduce readable hierarchy.
Preserve a continuous primary mass and clear solid-void hierarchy by merging or removing adjacent small cuts that have no independent role; do not invent a universal hole count or spacing.

Give base, middle and full-layer voids a visible support path appropriate to the material role; after translating, rotating or offsetting a cut volume, recheck joins, collisions, support and silhouette.

When a building grows in width, height or span, divide it into repeated column-beam bays with a continuous visible path from roof and floors through supports; do not uniformly stretch an unsegmented shell.

Align roof edges, feet or internal framing with beams, walls or columns; if the column grid blocks entrances, circulation or interior space, choose a span strategy suited to the design scale instead of simply deleting support.

Use connected diagonal braces where column-beam frames need lateral stability. Where arches imply horizontal thrust, use terrain abutment, thickened sides or buttresses. Match brace slope and thickness to scale and connect both ends.

Choose roof ridge orientation by comparing the resulting roof height and silhouette across candidate building axes; do not automatically apply the same orientation to every long edge, while preserving intentional exceptions.
Compose L-, T- or cross-plan roofs from connected components, fill their junction, remove duplicated overlaps, and align secondary roofs or dormers with the underlying volume or opening.

Budget border, ridge and stacked decoration into final roof height; express curved variants with slope phases that may steepen or flatten, choose block forms for scale, and avoid treating one demonstrated curve as a fixed template.

On even-width spans, close the roof by deliberately offsetting the ridge, changing one or both slope rhythms, or capping the top with a short flat or secondary structure; verify the silhouette instead of forcing a rigid peak.

For large or changing roof profiles, allow full blocks to form the primary surface when stair courses create striping or jagged transitions; use the wider full-block palette by color at distance, but recheck unusual textures close up.

Allocate roof detail selectively: combine ornate focal regions with clean roof areas or simpler roofs across a group, and reject decoration that overwhelms overall proportion or makes the surface uniformly busy.

When the brief calls for a modern flat or terrace roof, permit a bounded flat roof with a parapet instead of forcing a pitched profile; leave waterproofing and drainage unresolved rather than inventing them.
Recess facade infill behind its frame and, on larger walls, use additional bounded depth layers to create perspective and smaller readable regions before applying surface detail.
Establish readable base, beam and bracket support paths before optional facade ornament; preserve deliberate blank areas and reject detail that obscures the primary column or lacks a structural role.

Divide long walls into supported vertical bays, subdivide oversized bays with compatible partial components, and connect horizontal layers so they read as one facade rather than stacked unrelated walls.
Compose a window from an opening plus optional top weather hood, bottom sill or display ledge, and connected tension or compression supports; omit unneeded parts and integrate it with the wall frame.
Treat column base, shaft and capital as distinct optional zones; size their partial-block articulation to the column, and remove or simplify ornament when it becomes more prominent than the shaft.

When a facade cannot be recessed, use bounded partial-block relief within one block of depth; select attachment length and placement by building scale and junction role, and keep its palette coherent.
Choose door-panel, partial-block and frame materials by texture continuity and compatible connection states; use bounded head details to reduce a visually jagged gap between panel and frame.
Match entry detail to opening scale; for a large portal or small imprecise facade, permit a framed passable opening and omit a literal door panel, while using nested depth to retain hierarchy.
Connect a raised entrance to grade with a threshold or bounded stair sequence, and add a supported porch or canopy when the entry needs a waiting area that diverts rain away from the opening.
For a large open entry, compose exterior frame, vestibule or lobby, and inner threshold as a connected depth sequence; make the interior focal layer visible from outside without blocking circulation.

Use visually connective materials for continuous fields, denser smooth or bordered materials for supports, and distinctive directional or face-like textures only where scale makes their marks subordinate.
Build a large facade from a limited vocabulary of small line and relief units; combine repeat rhythms through shared alignments, and reject a unique element at every bay.
When shallow relief remains visually flat, increase facade volume to create deeper planes, then use their bounded shadow and value separation; surface-detail density cannot substitute for depth.

Develop a blank large wall through primary partition, role assignment, aligned secondary divisions and bounded detail; iterate proportions, remove unintended visual outliers, and preserve the planned solid-open hierarchy.

Plan the path and courtyard relationship before filling open ground; give planted features a plausible soil pocket and connect the resulting route, hard surface and vegetation without blocking circulation.
Blend soil, planting and hardscape with bounded mutual penetration rather than a hard material seam; keep a legible planting pocket and route while scattering only a limited edge band.
Compose landscape props as coherent clusters with one larger anchor and smaller subordinate pieces; group materials and implied uses, vary height front-to-back, and preserve clear walking space.

Derive road variation from traffic: concentrate fractured or worn material in traveled zones, retain less-damaged edges, and allow moss where movement is sparse instead of distributing noise uniformly.

Join road palettes and adjacent terrain with short, bidirectional material incursions; combine clustered and sparse replacements, soften the edge only enough to read as a transition, and keep the route legible.
Fit paths to terrain with a controlled vertical profile: use stairs for short steep rises, slabs for gentler grades, and partial blocks to smooth bends while maintaining a continuous passable route.

Build a tree from roots and a dominant trunk into thinner, alternating branches that spread in multiple directions; avoid equal-thickness radial arms and tune upper-versus-lower branch length to the intended crown.
Attach leaf masses to branches rather than wrapping the trunk; keep parts of the lower branch structure visible, place fuller foliage toward light-exposed zones, and use only bounded trunk foliage.
Vary tree orientation, crown density and silhouette within a coherent family; keep major crowns from collapsing into one repeated ball or overlapping into an unreadable mass.
Set bridge deck, navigation clearance and guard needs first; place supports at bends or visually weak spans with broadly regular spacing, without obstructing the required opening below.
Shape an arched bridge with gradually lengthening horizontal runs toward the center; adapt the step sequence to span width and reject abrupt straight-up, flat, straight-down profiles.

Complete bridge hierarchy in order—deck, supports, guards, then optional cover and accent—and stop adding underside detail once structure and safety read clearly; vary repeated materials to avoid fatigue.
Compose a water feature as bed, water-column and surface layers; preserve open water between clustered plants, bound plant heights, and distribute lighting only where the night composition needs it.
Choose aquatic inhabitants as a compatible set and provide the containment their movement requires; do not combine predator and prey populations or assume growing animals remain inside an open bank.

Carry shoreline materials across both water and land in bounded clusters and sparse fragments; use a stream mouth or sediment path when present to explain the gradient instead of drawing a hard bank seam.
Fit terrain around a building with bounded cuts and fills that extend beyond its exact footprint; replace deep right-angle excavation seams with staggered or curved terrain volumes.
Derive foundation masses from the building's major and minor footprint volumes, extend each toward grade, then add subordinate terrain chunks to break a tower-like or cross-shaped base.

Make building and foundation read as one system by embedding posts or walls into the base, matching their weathering and detail density, and echoing selected materials or vegetation across the boundary.
Organize a gap between buildings into optional foreground, mandatory ground contact, middle layer and high or distant layer; keep a stepped view through the zones rather than filling every depth.
Choose a porous tree or lattice when the rear scene should remain legible, and an opaque hedge or wall only when an unwanted view must be hidden; preserve depth cues instead of sealing every gap.
Connect neighboring buildings at ground, middle or upper level with a route, terrace or passable bridge that shares their material language; give elevated links visible support and usable clearance.
Select a valley site with distinct near, middle and far landforms plus open sight passages; balance enclosure with visual breathing room before assigning buildings or detailed scenery.

At large viewing distance, choose terrain materials primarily by color field and coverage; reserve texture-sensitive distinctions for closer layers and use continuous vegetation lines to interrupt exposed cliff bands.

Lay out a route hierarchy with different widths before placing valley buildings; use the resulting parcel size and shape to assign structures, planting or water, and transition paths visibly into ground.
Match outdoor seats, shade structures and stalls to the scene scale; use thinner assemblies for small fixtures and add support, thickness variation and deeper spans as their size increases.
Divide a beach into circulation, shade, rest, play, fishing or service zones before adding props; keep each cluster tied to its use and size decorative objects to the activity that produced them.
Break a broad sand field with bounded contrasting path, soil and vegetation patches, then blend each patch with related tones; contrast should clarify beach zones rather than become uniform noise.
Assign interior functions and circulation before furniture: place public, private and service zones by reachability, then size rooms and routes so each use remains legible and directly accessible.

Use a full partition only when privacy or enclosure requires it; otherwise divide zones with a partial-height screen, floor pattern or open frame that preserves sight lines and avoids a compressed room.
When the program and shell permit, connect floors with a bounded double-height void, gallery or overlook; use the shared volume for daylight or a suspended focal element.
Plan large stairs with the building framework and destination landings; in constrained rooms fold the run, use a spiral or ladder only where appropriate, and preserve circulation around it.
Place the room's largest function-bearing furniture first, attach secondary storage and work objects next, and reserve plants or tabletop items for the final pass; keep the circulation route clear.
Treat floor and ceiling as coordinated fields with bounded patterns, direction and material transitions; reuse block faces for their visual role while keeping the field subordinate to room zoning.

Reserve exterior wall access for rooms that need daylight, size windows to the available opening, and integrate frame, sill and optional screen with the wall palette instead of treating the window as an unrelated insert.

Build a small interior fixture from a readable primary object and a few role-bearing partial blocks; vary material or orientation to fit the room, but reject detail that obscures function or palette unity.
Compose a freestanding light as base, shaft and head; keep the base visually stable, transition from thick to thin with partial blocks or material changes, and size ornament to the total height.
Give every projecting lamp arm a visible bracket, curve or connection path back to its post, wall or ceiling; use the same support logic when adapting the assembly to an entrance or facade.
Arrange lamp heads symmetrically when repetition is intended, or balance unequal arms by opposing length and visual weight; reuse compatible post assemblies upside down for suspended lights.
Compose a chair from a seat surface and back, then add arms, headrest or upholstery only when scale and use support them; select partial blocks by shape, connection and palette rather than item name.

Use compact chairs where only a small footprint is available; increase scale to carry arms and layered support, and combine related seats into benches or sofas around a shared activity instead of isolated clutter.
Make a table legible through a usable tabletop plus its surrounding chairs, display or work context; choose a compact or full-block top according to footprint and whether objects must sit on it.
Separate a table from the floor with controlled value, texture or edge contrast; prefer calmer tabletop texture when a noisy material hides the outline, and coordinate it with the room palette.

For a carved dwelling, establish entrance, main route, smaller private rooms and a larger shared room before surface decoration; vary ceiling height to balance openness with the sheltering cave character.
After carving major cave rooms and level changes, establish a consistent visible support frame and reinforce corners, spans and galleries before wall, floor, storage or furniture finish passes.

Keep the cave base visually heavier than its ceiling, vary ceiling height in bounded zones, and distribute supported or concealed light by room size so dark areas are corrected without flattening all depth.
Use fewer transition levels for small color differences and more dense-to-sparse transition bands for large differences; keep the bounded material fields readable.
Apply structural subtraction, missing pieces and later additions to selected logical zones and key points; keep untreated structure readable instead of altering every surface.
Cluster greenery and organic growth in selected logical zones and key points; keep its coverage localized so it remains a layer of weathering rather than the whole design.

Resolve one representative structural facade bay as a unit wall, then repeat it with explicit connection faces and bounded variations so the large building retains one style without becoming mechanical.
Compose a large public building from a dominant hall and subordinate attached volumes, evaluating the silhouette from several approach angles before resolving repeated facade modules and roofs.
Plan the principal entrance, interior hall, platform and stairs as one circulation sequence; derive widths from use and structural rhythm rather than copying a fixed example dimension.
Give every building a logical route to a shared road or public space, merge wasteful parallel alleys, and use bends, branches and residual plots to organize the group.
Use terrain steps to arrange near-low and far-high layers, keep a landmark visible from primary routes, and reserve foreground clearance so adjacent roofs do not erase its silhouette.
Build a coherent family of house and tower templates, then vary height, width, diagonal form and placement; reduce exact reuse when the group requires greater refinement.
Declare primary observation points or travel paths before arranging volumes; keep foreground masses lower so important rear volumes remain visible, and spend detail where players can inspect it.
Use vegetation, small timber structures or terrain as bounded foreground occlusion for selected weak or blank areas, but leave the subject readable and still resolve exposed major surfaces.
Arrange successive low-to-high layers so each building is partly framed by the layer before it and becomes foreground for the layer behind, producing a continuous depth chain.
Reserve dense ornament for structurally or compositionally important zones and separate it with calmer wall fields, major columns and horizontal bands; full-surface ornament counts as no hierarchy.

Partition a repeated facade vertically and horizontally, alternate filled and quieter bays, and introduce purposeful openings or roof variants so repeat rhythm remains legible without exact full-field copying.
Choose current supported blocks by visual shape, face and material role, using partial-block assemblies only where they improve readable curves or transitions and not as automatic surface noise.
Lay out a diagonal rectangular envelope with a consistent step rhythm, build roof perimeter and ridge frames before infill, and count narrow-span parity so the roof closes cleanly.

Create a diagonal unit wall wide enough for a readable opening and support, repeat it on the step rhythm, and keep the envelope orthogonal in its own local frame rather than collapsing into a parallelogram.
Use a diagonal segment as a bounded accent within an otherwise stable building or group; prefer larger planar fields and simpler detail, and avoid making every volume diagonal.
